overview: Section D, the heaviest section of Part 3, covers what happens once engagement work is done. Internal auditors draft the final communication and later confirm that management carried out its actions; the chief audit executive approves and distributes results, judges whether management has accepted too much risk, and escalates. Management owns every fix, and the board decides on risk that stays unresolved. Most questions turn on who acts and in what order.
analogy: Think of a city's building inspection office. Inspectors write up each site visit, and before filing they walk the owner through what they found. The chief inspector signs every report and decides who gets a copy: the owner, the city engineer, sometimes the public. The owner, not the inspector, hires the builders, and the office later checks that repairs were done. If an owner keeps putting off a repair the city's code does not allow, the chief inspector raises it with the owner's head office and, if nothing changes, with the city council, which decides what happens next.

topics.overview: Standard 11.2 names seven qualities that every internal audit communication should have, and Standard 15.1 makes them a must for the final communication. This topic defines each quality, shows how to tell which one a weak draft breaks, and covers the methods the chief audit executive sets so the whole function writes this way.
can_do: Define each of the seven qualities as it applies to a final communication
Recognize which quality a flawed draft breaks, telling complete from concise and accurate from objective
Identify the methodologies a chief audit executive uses to make the function's communications effective

subtopics.name: Accurate, Objective and Complete
subtopics.definition: Accurate, objective and complete are the qualities about what a communication says: it is free of error, fair and balanced, and backed well enough that a reader would agree.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These three decide whether readers can trust the content. One wrong figure, loaded word or unsupported claim invites management to dispute everything else in the report.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 11.2 Effective Communication): the chief audit executive (CAE) sets methodologies that promote all seven qualities; Standard 15.1 requires them in every final communication.
Should (accurate): true to the facts, with no errors or distortions, using precise terms that the information gathered supports.
Should (objective): impartial, resting on a balanced look at all relevant facts, linked to objectives, and free of wording that reads as biased.
Should (complete): enough relevant, reliable and sufficient support that a reader would reach the auditors' conclusion; it does not mean every detail.
Should: fit the content to what each recipient needs in order to act; the board's needs differ from those of the activity's managers.
subtopics.example: Auditor Lerato drafts a finding on overtime at a bus operator in Durban: 'Depot managers abused overtime, costing millions.' The supervisor flags three problems: 'abused' is loaded, the true figure is 1.2 million rand, and the sample behind the claim is missing. Lerato rewrites it with the exact figure, neutral wording and the sample results, then resubmits it for review.

review: Sample issued reports and trace key figures to the workpapers
Inspect report wording for loaded or blaming terms
evidence: Supervisory review notes raised on draft communications
Stakeholder survey results on report fairness and accuracy
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive add accuracy and balance checks to the supervisory review of every draft.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive approves the final wording before issue

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: every final communication is accurate, objective and complete, along with the other four qualities (Standard 15.1). Complete means enough support for the reader to reach the same conclusion, not every detail. Objective means balanced, not soft.

exam_traps.trap: A complete report lists every test performed and every exception found, however minor.
exam_traps.why: Complete means enough relevant, reliable and sufficient support to reach the conclusion. Needless detail breaks the concise quality instead.

exam_traps.trap: To stay objective, a report should say nothing about what the activity does well.
exam_traps.why: Objective means balanced. Assurance conclusions acknowledge effective processes (Standard 14.5), and the CAE should encourage auditors to recognize good performance (Standard 11.3).

key_terms.definition: A statement that bends the facts it reports, such as an exaggerated figure or trend that the evidence does not support.
Words that judge or blame, such as 'negligent', where a neutral description of the facts would do.

subtopics.memory_aid: Right facts, fair view, enough proof: accurate, objective, complete.

subtopics.name: Clear, Concise, Constructive and Timely
subtopics.definition: Clear, concise, constructive and timely are the qualities about how and when results arrive: easy to follow, free of padding, helpful in tone, and in time to act.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A correct finding still fails if readers cannot follow it, give up halfway, feel attacked, or receive it after the damage is done.
how_it_works: Should (clear): logical and easy for the intended reader, in the organization's own terms, with unusual terms defined and significant supporting details kept.
Should (concise): no repetition and nothing unnecessary, insignificant or unrelated to the engagement; the aim is no waste, not the fewest pages.
Should (constructive): helpful to the organization, in a cooperative tone that invites the activity's management to work on improvements with the auditors.
Should (timely): delivered when the issue's significance calls for it, early enough for management to act; what counts as timely varies by engagement.
Should (Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication): raise issues needing immediate attention during the engagement; the final communication is not the first warning.
subtopics.example: At a seed cooperative in Rosario, auditor Valentina's draft on grain-moisture testing runs to 30 pages, uses lab codes throughout and is four months past fieldwork. The supervisor returns it. Valentina cuts repeated sections, replaces codes with plain names, changes 'staff failed' to 'the test step was skipped' and sets an issue date two weeks away.

review: Compare report issue dates with fieldwork end dates
Inspect drafts for technical terms left undefined
evidence: Report timeliness measures tracked by the function
Recipient feedback on clarity and usefulness of reports
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set a target time from fieldwork end to report issue and track it.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive sets timeliness targets in the methodology

subtopics.isaca_rule: Write for the reader who must act: plain terms, no padding, a helpful tone, and in time for action. Timely follows the issue's significance; it is never speed bought at the cost of accuracy.

exam_traps.trap: The most timely report is the one issued fastest, even before review is complete.
exam_traps.why: Timely means suited to the issue's significance so management can act. All seven qualities apply together, and the chief audit executive approves the final communication before issue (Standard 15.1).

exam_traps.trap: Constructive means softening a serious finding so management is not upset.
exam_traps.why: Constructive is a helpful, cooperative tone aimed at improvement. The substance stays accurate and objective: a serious finding is still stated as serious.

key_terms.definition: Specialist words or codes the intended reader does not use, which should be avoided or defined.
Everyday words and short sentences that the intended reader understands on first reading.

subtopics.name: Telling the Qualities Apart in a Draft
subtopics.definition: Recognizing the qualities in practice means reading a real draft and naming which quality a weakness breaks, especially where two qualities sound alike.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam options often swap two similar qualities. Naming the right one also points to the right fix: more support, less padding, fairer words or faster delivery.
how_it_works: KaiSip's reading: ask what fix the flaw needs: a fact corrected (accurate), balance restored (objective), support added (complete) or material cut (concise).
KaiSip's reading: complete and concise pull different ways without clashing; give all the support the conclusion needs and nothing beyond it.
KaiSip's reading: accurate asks whether the facts are right; objective asks whether the facts chosen, and the words used, are fair.
KaiSip's reading: clear asks whether the reader understands; a short report full of jargon is concise but not clear.
Should (Standard 11.3 Communicating Results): the chief audit executive (CAE) encourages acknowledging satisfactory performance, which supports balance, not softness.

rows.label: Complete or concise
cells: Complete adds needed support; concise removes what is not needed
Would cutting this change the reader's conclusion?

rows.label: Accurate or objective
cells: Accurate is about correct facts; objective is about fair choice of facts and words
Is it wrong, or one-sided?

rows.label: Clear or concise
cells: Clear is about understanding; concise is about length and repetition
Is the reader lost, or just reading too much?

rows.label: Timely or fast
cells: Timely fits the issue's significance and leaves time to act
Can management still act on it?

rows.label: Constructive or soft
cells: Constructive is a helpful tone; soft changes the substance
Did a fact or rating change?

subtopics.example: Supervisor Haruto at a rail operator in Osaka reviews three drafts. One lists all 400 sampled tickets in the body; another calls a station manager 'careless'; a third says 'about half' where the workpaper shows 38 percent. Haruto marks them concise, objective and accurate in turn, and asks each auditor to fix only that flaw.

review: Sample review notes and classify each by the quality raised
Compare recurring review-note themes across auditors and engagements
evidence: Review-note log grouped by communication quality
Training records on report writing for each auditor
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive aim writing training at the qualities that review notes flag most often.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides training and style guide changes

subtopics.isaca_rule: Name the flaw by the fix it needs: add support (complete), cut padding (concise), correct a fact (accurate), rebalance (objective), explain (clear), retone (constructive), deliver while action is still possible (timely).

exam_traps.trap: A finding that leaves out the sample behind it is a concise finding.
exam_traps.why: Leaving out support the conclusion rests on makes it incomplete. Concise removes what is unnecessary, never what the reader needs to reach the conclusion.

exam_traps.trap: A report containing a wrong figure fails the objective quality.
exam_traps.why: A wrong figure breaks accuracy. Objective concerns balance and fair wording; a report can be right in every figure and still one-sided.

key_terms.definition: A fact or test result that a reader needs in order to accept a finding or conclusion.
A judgment that weighs all relevant facts, including those that favor the activity under review.

subtopics.memory_aid: What it says: accurate, objective, complete. How and when: clear, concise, constructive, timely.

subtopics.name: Methodologies for Effective Communication
subtopics.definition: Communication methodologies are the chief audit executive's documented policies, templates, style rules, review steps and training that make the function's communications meet the seven qualities consistently.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a shared method, quality depends on who drafted the report. Methodologies make good communication repeatable across auditors and measurable over time.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 11.2): the chief audit executive (CAE) establishes and implements methodologies that promote the seven qualities.
May: methodologies include policies, criteria, style guides and procedures.
Should: methodologies reflect what the board, senior management and other stakeholders expect, and supervisory review tests each draft against the qualities.
Should (Standard 13.1): use formal, informal, written and oral methods; oral presentations are usually backed by a written or digital copy.
May: the CAE trains auditors in writing and presenting, and sets communication measures, such as timeliness, for the quality program.
subtopics.example: After audit committee members at a water utility in Lima say reports are hard to use, chief audit executive Rosa issues a two-page template that opens with the conclusion, adds a style guide of plain terms, runs a writing workshop for the team, and starts measuring the days from fieldwork end to issue.

review: Inspect the methodology for a style guide, templates and review steps
Compare a sample of recent reports with the template
evidence: Timeliness and survey scores tracked for each issued report
Board and stakeholder survey results on report usefulness
Attendance records for writing training
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive confirm with the board that report format and frequency meet its expectations.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive sets the methodology, informed by board expectations

subtopics.isaca_rule: Effective communication is a function-wide method, not a personal talent. The CAE must set methodologies for the seven qualities, should fit them to stakeholder expectations, and may measure them in the quality program.

exam_traps.trap: Each auditor should choose the report format that suits their own writing style.
exam_traps.why: Methodologies such as templates and style guides give consistency across the function, so the board reads every report the same way.

exam_traps.trap: A written report is the only acceptable way to deliver engagement results.
exam_traps.why: Formal, informal, written and oral methods all have a place, and several versions may suit different audiences. Oral presentations are usually backed by a copy.

key_terms.definition: The function's written rules for how its communications are worded and laid out.
A standard layout for a communication, such as a findings form or report outline, that auditors fill in.

topics.overview: The final communication is the engagement's lasting record and the basis for follow-up. Internal auditors draft it and the chief audit executive approves it before issue. This topic covers its required parts, how findings are written into it, when it may state that the work conformed with the Standards, and when a scope limitation must be explained in it.
can_do: Draft the required parts of a final communication for an assurance engagement and for an advisory one
Write a finding with its significance, owner and target date, acknowledging action management has already taken
Recognize when the conformance statement may be used and what must be disclosed instead
Identify when a scope limitation must be explained in the final communication

subtopics.name: Required Parts of the Final Communication
subtopics.definition: The required parts of a final communication are the content Standard 15.1 sets for every engagement, plus the extra content that an assurance engagement must carry.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Readers learn from it what was examined, what was found and who will act by when. A missing scope can make a conclusion look broader than the work.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 15.1 Final Engagement Communication): every final communication gives the objectives, scope and conclusions, plus recommendations or action plans where there are any.
Must, assurance only: findings with their significance and priority, an explanation of any scope limitation, and a conclusion on governance, risk management and control effectiveness.
Must: name the people who will deal with the findings and the date by which action is planned, and acknowledge actions management has started or completed.
Must: internal auditors make sure the chief audit executive (CAE) reviews and approves it before issue. The CAE then decides who receives it (see 3D4.2).
May: add a title, background, recognition of good practice or cooperation, and a distribution list; the CAE may supply templates.

rows.label: Every engagement
cells: Objectives, scope, conclusions, any recommendations or action plans, owners and dates, actions already taken
Title, background, recognition, distribution list

rows.label: Assurance engagement adds
cells: Findings with significance and priority, any scope limitation, a conclusion on effectiveness
An overall rating on the function's scale (see 3D5.3)

subtopics.example: Auditor Tomasz drafts the final communication for a pharmacy-stock assurance engagement at a hospital group in Gdansk. The draft has findings and a conclusion but no scope and no dates. Tomasz adds the sites and months covered, the significance and priority of each finding, each owner and target date, and the conclusion on control effectiveness, then sends it to the chief audit executive for approval.

review: Sample final communications against the required content list
Compare report issue dates with the recorded approval dates
evidence: Approval records for each final communication before issue
Report checklists completed by the engagement team
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive build every required part into the report template and review checklist.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive signs off; management owns the listed actions

subtopics.isaca_rule: Every engagement: objectives, scope, conclusions, any recommendations or action plans, owners and dates. Assurance adds findings ranked by significance, scope limitations and a conclusion on effectiveness. Internal auditors draft; the CAE approves before issue.

exam_traps.trap: An advisory engagement's final communication needs no stated scope or conclusion.
exam_traps.why: Objectives, scope and conclusions are required for every engagement. Findings with priority, scope limitations and the effectiveness conclusion are the assurance-only additions.

exam_traps.trap: Owners and dates can be left for the follow-up tracking system to record.
exam_traps.why: Must: the final communication itself names who will address the findings and the planned completion date (Standard 15.1).

key_terms.definition: The communication issued at the end of an engagement with its results, often a written report.
The people and bodies named in a report as its recipients, as decided by the chief audit executive.

subtopics.memory_aid: Every report: what, how far, so what, who and when. Assurance adds ranked findings and limits.

subtopics.name: Writing Findings, Owners and Dates
subtopics.definition: A written finding sets out, in plain language, the criteria, the condition, the root cause, the effect and the significance, then the agreed action with its owner and date.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Management acts on the finding as written. A finding that skips the cause, the owner or the date invites a quick patch that nobody owns and nobody can follow up.
how_it_works: May (Standard 14.3): the chief audit executive (CAE) provides a findings template; how criteria, condition, cause, effect and significance are judged is Part 2 (2B6.1 to 2B6.3).
Should: write findings succinctly and plainly, so the activity's management understands the gap and the evidence behind its significance.
Must (Standard 15.1): give assurance findings their significance and priority, and name the person responsible and the planned completion date.
Must: acknowledge in the communication any action management started or completed before issue (see 3D4.4).
Should (Standard 11.3): acknowledge satisfactory performance, especially a practice other units could copy.
subtopics.example: Auditor Imani writes up a finding at a microfinance lender in Nairobi: loan officers approved 14 loans above their limit (condition) against a policy cap (criteria), because the system does not block them (root cause), exposing the lender to bad debt (effect). Imani rates it high, records the operations head as owner with a 31 March date, and notes that limits were reset last week.

review: Inspect a sample of issued findings for every template element
Trace report action owners into tracking system entries
evidence: Completed findings templates in the workpapers
Tracking system entries matching report owners and dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive require a named owner and date on every finding before approval.
audit_focus.decides: Management names the owner and commits to the completion date

subtopics.isaca_rule: Write each finding so a manager could act on it alone: the gap, why it happened, why it matters, how serious it is, who will fix it and by when, and what is already done.

exam_traps.trap: The internal auditor who raised a finding should be named as its action owner, to keep follow-up simple.
exam_traps.why: Management owns and implements actions (Standard 14.4). The final communication names the responsible manager; internal auditors later confirm implementation.

exam_traps.trap: Findings should list every exception in full to prove the point.
exam_traps.why: Findings should be succinct and plain, with the evidence that supports their significance. Long exception lists usually belong in the workpapers.

key_terms.definition: The manager named in the final communication as responsible for carrying out an action.
The date, stated in the final communication, by which management expects an action to be done.

subtopics.name: The Conformance Statement
subtopics.definition: The conformance statement is a sentence in a final communication saying the engagement followed the Global Internal Audit Standards; it is used only when the evidence supports it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It tells readers they can rely on the work's quality. Making it without support misleads them; Standard 1.3's considerations list an unsupported claim that the function conforms as discreditable conduct.
how_it_works: Should (Standard 15.1, a consideration): include a statement that the engagement was performed in conformance with the Global Internal Audit Standards.
Should: use it only when the results of engagement supervision and of the quality assurance and improvement program support it.
Must (Standard 15.1): if the engagement did not conform, disclose the standards not met, the reasons, and the impact on findings and conclusions (function level: 3C2).
Must (Standard 4.1): if other bodies' requirements were also followed, the communication cites them as appropriate.
Must (Standard 4.1): where a law stops conformance with part of the Standards, conform with every other part and make appropriate disclosures.

rows.label: Supervision and the quality program support conformance
cells: Yes, it should be included
The statement

rows.label: A standard was not met on this engagement
cells: No
The standards not met, the reasons and the impact on findings and conclusions

rows.label: Another body's requirements also applied
cells: Yes, if supported
The statement, and a citation of the other requirements

subtopics.example: At a state pension fund in Abuja, a regulator's fixed deadline means the supervisor's review of key fund-transfer workpapers cannot be finished. Chief audit executive Oyelaran removes the conformance statement from the draft and adds a disclosure naming the standard not met, the reason, and how it may affect the findings and conclusions.

review: Sample reports carrying the statement and trace supervision sign-offs
Compare statements used with the latest quality assessment results
evidence: Supervisory sign-offs for engagements whose reports claim conformance
Internal and external quality assessment conclusions
Nonconformance disclosures in issued final communications
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive permit the statement only after supervision and quality results are checked.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive judges whether the evidence supports conformance

subtopics.isaca_rule: The statement is a should, and only with support from supervision and the quality program. The must runs the other way: an engagement that did not conform discloses which standard, why, and the impact on findings and conclusions.

exam_traps.trap: Every final communication must state that the engagement conformed with the Standards.
exam_traps.why: Including the statement is a consideration, a should, and only when supervision and quality results support it. The requirement is to disclose nonconformance when it happens.

exam_traps.trap: A small nonconformance can be left out if the conclusion still stands.
exam_traps.why: Must: a nonconformance on the engagement is disclosed with the standards, reasons and impact. The impact may be small, but it is still stated.

key_terms.definition: A 'should' or 'may' in a standard: preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.
Meeting the requirements of the Global Internal Audit Standards.
A requirement of the Standards that was not met; it is documented and disclosed as the Standards direct.

subtopics.memory_aid: Claim conformance only with proof. Missed a standard? Say which, why and what it changed.

subtopics.name: Scope Limitations in the Final Communication
subtopics.definition: Documenting a scope limitation means explaining in the final communication which planned assurance work could not be done, why, and how that narrows the conclusion.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A conclusion that hides a limitation claims more than the work supports, and readers may rely on assurance nobody gave.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 15.1): the assurance final communication explains any scope limitation, and the conclusion reaches only as far as the work done.
Must (Standard 13.3): the chief audit executive (CAE) elevates a limitation management does not resolve to the board; spotting and discussing one is Part 2 (2A1.3, 2C2.3).
KaiSip's reading: a stakeholder request that the auditors judged to be a limitation is explained in the report like any other.
Must (Standard 11.3): a conclusion at business unit or organization level states its scope, including limitations and the period covered.
subtopics.example: In a payroll assurance engagement at a shipping line in Piraeus, the crewing agency refuses auditors access to sea-staff timesheets, and talks with management fail. Chief audit executive Eleni raises it with the board, which has not acted by the report date. Eleni approves a final communication that explains the missing timesheets and limits the conclusion to onshore payroll.

review: Trace scope limitations in the workpapers to their explanation in reports
Compare report conclusions with the scope actually tested
evidence: Workpaper log of scope limitations with discussion and outcome
Board minutes recording limitations the chief audit executive elevated
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive add a scope limitation section to the assurance report template.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides whether to intervene in an unresolved limitation

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: an assurance final communication explains any scope limitation, and its conclusion reaches no further than the work done. An unresolved one also goes from the CAE to the board. Silence about a limitation overstates the assurance.

exam_traps.trap: Once the board has been told of a scope limitation, the report need not mention it.
exam_traps.why: Elevating a limitation and reporting it are separate duties. The assurance final communication must still explain it to every reader (Standard 15.1).

exam_traps.trap: The untested area looked low risk, so the conclusion can still cover the whole activity.
exam_traps.why: The conclusion reaches only as far as the work done. The untested area is explained as a scope limitation, not assumed sound (Standard 15.1).

key_terms.definition: A condition in an assurance engagement, such as restricted access, that prevents the planned work.
What an engagement will and will not cover.

topics.overview: After evaluating findings, internal auditors decide whether to recommend a fix, ask management for an action plan, or agree actions together, and then judge whether the proposed action will work at a sensible cost. This topic also covers the protocol when management disagrees with a finding or a plan. Management owns and carries out every action.
can_do: Determine whether to develop a recommendation, request an action plan or agree actions with management in a scenario
Weigh a proposed action's cost against the risk it reduces and the organization's risk tolerance
Determine whether an action plan reaches the root cause or only treats the symptom
Recognize the protocol when management disagrees with a finding or an action plan

subtopics.name: Recommend, Request or Agree
subtopics.definition: Choosing the route means deciding whether internal auditors propose a fix, ask management to design its own action plan, or work with management to agree actions together.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The route shapes ownership. A good fit gives management a plan it believes in, while auditors keep their judgment of whether it works.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 14.4 Recommendations and Action Plans): internal auditors determine whether to recommend, request an action plan or agree actions with management.
Must (Standard 14.4): choose the route with its aims in view: close the criteria-condition gap, cut risk to an acceptable level, deal with the root cause, improve the activity.
Must: discuss any recommendation with the management of the activity under review.
May: give one specific recommendation, several options, or ask management to research options and choose. One finding may need several actions.
Should (Standard 14.4): internal auditors collaborate on actions but leave implementing them to management, whose responsibility it is.
KaiSip's reading: the table shows when each route tends to fit. The Standards set no fixed test for choosing.

rows.label: Develop a recommendation
cells: The fix is specific and the auditors can see it clearly
Management still owns and implements it

rows.label: Request an action plan
cells: Management knows the process best and several fixes could work
Test the plan against the root cause and tolerance

rows.label: Agree actions together
cells: The issue is complex or crosses units and needs both views
Collaboration must not slide into designing the process

subtopics.example: At a hotel chain in Bali, auditor Wayan finds night clerks approving refunds above policy limits. The fix is specific, so Wayan recommends blocking clerk approvals above the limit in the booking system. For a second finding, weak supplier vetting across three hotels, several approaches could work, so Wayan asks the regional operations director for an action plan.

review: Sample findings for the route chosen and the reason recorded
Trace each recommendation to a recorded discussion with management
evidence: Notes of findings discussions with authorized managers
Delegation rules showing which managers may commit to actions
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive define which management level may agree action plans for each kind of finding.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the chosen action and carries it out

subtopics.isaca_rule: Pick the route most likely to get the root cause fixed by the people who own it. Whatever the route, internal auditors discuss it with management, and management implements.

exam_traps.trap: Requesting an action plan is weaker than recommending, so auditors should always write the recommendation.
exam_traps.why: The Standards give three routes and rank none. Management's own plan may fit best when it knows the process and several fixes could work.

exam_traps.trap: When management has no ideas, the internal auditor should write and run the action plan.
exam_traps.why: Auditors may offer options or recommend, but management owns and implements actions. Designing and running the fix would take on a management responsibility.

key_terms.definition: An action internal auditors propose to close a gap, reduce a risk or improve the activity under review.
Management's stated steps to deal with a finding, with a named owner and a target date.

subtopics.name: Cost, Benefit and Feasibility
subtopics.definition: Weighing cost and benefit means checking that a proposed action is practical and costs no more than the risk reduction justifies, while still bringing the risk within tolerance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An action that costs more than the risk wastes money and rarely gets done. One that is cheap but leaves risk above tolerance does not solve the problem.
how_it_works: Should (Standard 14.4): evaluate and discuss with management whether recommendations or action plans are feasible and reasonable, including a cost-benefit analysis.
Should: test whether the action deals with the risk satisfactorily under the organization's risk tolerance, not only whether it is affordable.
May (Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication): the closing communication can weigh how severe the risk is against what acting would cost and gain.
Sound practice: count all costs, such as money, staff time, slower processing and new risks, and all benefits, such as losses avoided.
Sound practice: keep the cost-benefit reasoning in the workpapers; Standard 14.3 lists such a workpaper among its examples of evidence of conformance.
subtopics.example: At a regional airline in Fiji, auditor Sefa finds that fuel invoices are not matched to delivery tickets. Management proposes hiring two clerks to check every invoice, costing more than a year's typical loss. Sefa discusses a cheaper option, an automatic match with exception review that brings the risk within the airline's tolerance, and records both options in the workpapers.

review: Inspect workpapers for a cost-benefit analysis behind major recommendations
Compare agreed actions with the risk tolerance they must meet
evidence: Workpapers quantifying each option's cost and expected loss avoided
Notes of feasibility discussions with management
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive require a recorded cost-benefit view for every significant recommendation.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses and funds the action it will take

subtopics.isaca_rule: A good action is feasible, proportionate and enough: its cost fits the risk, and it brings the risk within tolerance. Should: evaluate feasibility and cost against benefit, and discuss both with management.

exam_traps.trap: The best recommendation removes the risk completely, whatever it costs.
exam_traps.why: Should: actions are weighed for feasibility and for cost against benefit. The aim is risk within tolerance, not zero risk at any price.

exam_traps.trap: If management finds every action too costly, the finding should be dropped.
exam_traps.why: Cost shapes the choice of action, not the finding. If management will not act and the risk stays above appetite or tolerance, the risk acceptance route applies (see 3D6).

key_terms.definition: Comparing what an action costs with the loss or harm it is expected to prevent.
Whether an action can realistically be carried out with the organization's people, systems, money and time.

subtopics.name: Testing an Action Plan Against the Root Cause
subtopics.definition: Testing an action plan means judging whether management's proposed steps remove the underlying cause of a finding, rather than only correcting the instances that were found.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A plan that fixes only the symptom lets the gap come back, and the same finding reappears at the next engagement.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 14.3): identify root causes with management when possible. Standard 14.4 names addressing the root cause as one aim of the actions.
Sound practice: ask of each step whether it changes why the gap happened, or only repairs the items found.
Sound practice: a sound plan names an owner with authority, a realistic date and an outcome that can later be checked.
Should (Standard 14.4): confirm that the plan deals with the risk satisfactorily under the organization's risk tolerance.
Sound practice: correcting the exceptions found is often needed too, but on its own it treats the symptom.

rows.label: Unapproved journal entries
cells: Get approval for the 20 entries found
Set the system to block posting without approval

rows.label: Late reconciliations
cells: Finish the overdue reconciliations
Reassign the work and add a due-date alert

rows.label: Staff skip a checklist step
cells: Email staff a reminder
Build the step into the system and the supervisor's review

subtopics.example: At a cement maker in Monterrey, auditor Lucia finds 30 weighbridge tickets altered without supervisor sign-off. The plant manager plans to re-check those 30 tickets. Asking why, Lucia learns that any operator can edit a ticket after printing. Lucia tells the manager the plan treats the symptom and asks for steps that restrict edits, with an owner and a date.

review: Compare each action plan with the root cause in the workpapers
Sample later engagements for findings that recurred after closure
evidence: Root cause analysis recorded for each finding
Repeat-finding analysis across engagements
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive track repeat findings as a sign that action plans miss root causes.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides the final action plan and owns its delivery

subtopics.isaca_rule: An action plan passes when it changes why the gap happened, has an owner and a date, and brings the risk within tolerance. Repairing the items found is a start, not a fix.

exam_traps.trap: Correcting every exception found closes the finding.
exam_traps.why: That fixes the instances found. Unless the cause changes, new exceptions follow; the actions should address the root cause (Standard 14.4).

exam_traps.trap: If the auditor judges the plan weak, the auditor should rewrite it for management.
exam_traps.why: Internal auditors explain why the plan falls short and may suggest options. Management revises and owns the plan.

key_terms.definition: The deeper reason a gap exists, as opposed to its visible symptom.
A finding that reappears in a later engagement, often a sign that the earlier action missed the cause.

subtopics.memory_aid: Fix the why, not just the what.

subtopics.name: When Management Disagrees
subtopics.definition: The disagreement protocol is the set route internal auditors follow when management disputes a finding, a conclusion, a recommendation or an action plan.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a set route, a dispute stalls the report or pushes auditors to soften results; the protocol keeps results honest.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.1): discuss the disagreement with the activity's management and seek mutual understanding; results need not change without a valid reason, such as new evidence.
Must (Standards 13.1, 14.4): follow the established methodology that lets both parties state their positions and reasons, and determine a resolution.
Should: the chief audit executive (CAE) works with senior management to help settle a dispute over engagement results; management still decides its own actions.
May: attach each party's formal statement to the final communication, or make it available on request.
Must (Standard 8.1 Board Interaction): if a disagreement may affect the function's ability to do its work, the CAE gives the board the facts.
KaiSip's reading: settling a dispute over results is not resolving a risk; refusing to act on risk above appetite or tolerance goes the 3D6 route.

rows.label: 1. Discuss and seek mutual understanding
cells: Internal auditors with the activity's management
Must

rows.label: 2. State both positions under the methodology
cells: Internal auditors and management
Must

rows.label: 3. Help resolve what remains
cells: The CAE with senior management
Should

rows.label: 4. Give the board the facts, if the function's work is affected
cells: The CAE
Must

subtopics.example: At a telecom in Lusaka, the billing director rejects a finding on unbilled prepaid top-ups, saying the test used old data. Auditor Chanda reruns it on current data, gets the same result and keeps the finding. The director's written response is attached to the final communication.

review: Trace disputed findings to the record of both positions
Compare draft and final wording of disputed findings for unexplained softening
evidence: Management responses attached to final communications
Version history of disputed findings with reasons for edits
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive document the disagreement route and when management responses are attached.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides its response; the chief audit executive approves the final wording

subtopics.isaca_rule: Discuss, seek mutual understanding, record both positions; results need not change without a valid reason and are never softened. The CAE should work with senior management on what remains; the board gets the facts when the function's work is affected.

exam_traps.trap: To keep the relationship, revise the finding's rating until management accepts it.
exam_traps.why: Results change only for a valid reason. Softening a finding to end a dispute undermines objectivity; both positions are recorded instead.

exam_traps.trap: The internal auditor should take any disagreement straight to the board.
exam_traps.why: Discuss with management and follow the methodology first; the CAE should work with senior management. The board hears only disagreements affecting the function's work.

key_terms.definition: Both sides see the facts and their meaning the same way, even if they differ on what to do.
A sound basis for changing results, such as new evidence or a factual error, as opposed to pressure or preference.

subtopics.memory_aid: Discuss, record both, change only for a reason; CAE with senior management; board if the function is hit.

topics.overview: Results are finalized with management at the closing communication. The chief audit executive then approves the final communication and decides who receives it and in what form. This topic covers the exit conference, the chief audit executive's distribution duty, what each audience needs, how to report a finding already fixed, and how to correct a significant error.
can_do: Describe the purpose of the closing communication and who takes part
Recognize the chief audit executive's duties to approve and distribute results and to seek advice before an outside release
Recognize what each stakeholder group needs from engagement results
Describe how to report a finding already resolved and how to correct a significant error or omission

subtopics.name: The Closing Communication
subtopics.definition: The closing communication, often called the exit conference, is a meeting where internal auditors and the activity's management finalize the engagement results before the final communication is issued.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It brings out factual errors and disagreements while they can still be settled, and it gets action plans, owners and dates confirmed before results reach senior management and the board.
how_it_works: May (Standard 13.1, considerations): depending on the engagement, internal auditors hold a closing communication with the activity's managers and the staff concerned.
May: its purpose is to finalize results, discuss differences with the goal of agreement, and test whether recommendations or action plans are feasible.
May: management can bring early ideas rather than finished plans; afterward it confirms its action plans, timing and the people responsible.
Must (Standard 13.1): a dispute raised there follows the disagreement protocol (3D3.4); where the meeting sits among engagement messages is Part 2 (2C2.2).
Sound practice: record who attended, what was agreed and what is still disputed, and file it in the workpapers.
subtopics.example: At the closing meeting for a cold-chain engagement at a dairy in Christchurch, auditor Aroha, the plant manager and two shift leads go through the draft findings. A shift lead shows that one temperature gap was a sensor fault already logged, so Aroha corrects it. The manager confirms owners and dates for two actions, and Aroha files the minutes.

review: Compare closing meeting minutes with the findings in the final communication
Trace findings changed after closing to a recorded valid reason
evidence: Attendance records and agreed points from each exit conference
Management confirmations of action plans, owners and dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set when a closing communication is held and how it is recorded.
audit_focus.decides: Management commits to the actions; the chief audit executive approves final results

subtopics.isaca_rule: The closing communication finalizes results with the people who run the activity: correct facts, air disagreements, confirm actions. It is a discussion of evidence, not a bargaining session over conclusions.

exam_traps.trap: The exit conference is where auditors negotiate a conclusion management will accept.
exam_traps.why: It aims at agreement on facts and actions, but results need not change without a valid reason. A conclusion is never traded for cooperation.

exam_traps.trap: Every engagement must end with a formal exit conference.
exam_traps.why: The Standards say a closing communication may be held, depending on the engagement. The requirement is to communicate effectively throughout (Standard 13.1).

key_terms.definition: A discussion before the final communication, also called an exit conference, where auditors and management finalize the results.
Employees of the activity under review who can confirm facts or will carry out actions, invited alongside its managers.

subtopics.name: Approving and Distributing the Final Communication
subtopics.definition: Distribution is the chief audit executive's duty to approve each final communication and decide who receives it, and how, so results reach people who will give them due consideration.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A sound report sent to the wrong people, or to nobody with authority, changes nothing. One sent outside without advice can breach law or confidentiality.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 11.3 Communicating Results): the chief audit executive (CAE) reviews and approves final communications and decides recipients and method before issue.
May: the CAE delegates these duties to other internal auditors.
Must: the CAE keeps overall responsibility when delegating.
Must (Standard 15.1): the CAE disseminates results to parties who can ensure due consideration; these may include the board, senior management and action owners.
Must (Standard 11.3): before a release outside the organization, seek advice from legal counsel, senior management or both as required, unless law sets otherwise.
Must (Standards 8.1, 11.3): report results to the board and senior management periodically and per engagement as appropriate, including themes across engagements.
subtopics.example: Joaquin, chief audit executive of a retail bank in Montevideo, approves a final communication on card fraud controls. Joaquin sends it to the head of cards and the chief operating officer and puts a summary in the next audit committee pack. When the card network's assessor asks for a copy, Joaquin consults legal counsel before releasing an agreed extract.

review: Compare each report's actual recipients with its approved distribution
Trace each external release to a documented clearance before the send date
evidence: Distribution records with approver and date for each report
Clearance memos from counsel for reports shared outside
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set distribution rules by report type and a procedure for outside releases.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a delegate, settles the recipient list

subtopics.isaca_rule: Internal auditors draft; the CAE approves and decides who receives results and how, keeping responsibility even when delegating. Results go to those who can act or oversee; an outside release follows any required legal or senior management advice.

exam_traps.trap: The engagement auditor decides who receives the report, since they know the area best.
exam_traps.why: Must: the CAE decides to whom and how final communications are disseminated (Standard 11.3), and stays responsible even when delegating the task.

exam_traps.trap: The CAE needs the board's approval before any report leaves the organization.
exam_traps.why: Before an outside release the CAE must seek advice from legal counsel, senior management or both as required. The Standard does not require board approval.

key_terms.definition: Sending a final communication to its chosen recipients, in the form the chief audit executive decides.
Serious attention to results from people with the authority to act on them or oversee them.

subtopics.memory_aid: Auditors draft; the CAE approves, picks the readers and clears outside releases.

subtopics.name: Different Audiences, Different Needs
subtopics.definition: Audience fit means shaping the content, format and detail of results for each recipient, according to what they know, how they are affected and what they must do.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The activity's managers need detail to act, the board needs the overall picture to oversee, and outside parties may receive only what law and policy allow.
how_it_works: Should (Standard 11.2): adapt each communication to what its recipient needs for the actions they are responsible for.
May (Standard 15.1): issue several versions of a final communication, varying format, content and detail by audience.
Must (Standard 8.1): give the board what it needs for oversight, whether it asked or not.
May (Standard 9.5): coordination can include giving other assurance providers, such as risk management or external auditors, access to reports.
Must (Standard 1.3): make the disclosures law requires, such as to regulators; public sector law may require results at public meetings.

rows.label: Management of the activity under review
cells: Each finding, its cause and actions, in detail
Full report and closing discussion

rows.label: Senior management
cells: Significant findings, themes, action progress
Summary and briefings

rows.label: The board
cells: Conclusions, significant risks, themes, action status
Committee papers

rows.label: Other assurance providers (risk management, external auditors)
cells: Results that affect their own work
Agreed access to reports

rows.label: Regulators and the public
cells: Only what law or approved policy requires
Release after required advice

subtopics.example: After an emissions-data engagement at a steel maker in Linz, chief audit executive Katharina sends plant managers the full report, gives the executive board a one-page summary, shares results with risk management for its register, and on legal counsel's advice gives the regulator the section its permit requires.

review: Compare versions of one report sent to different audiences for consistency
Inspect board papers for conclusions, themes and action status
evidence: Report versions with their recipient lists
Board minutes showing engagement results discussed
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive confirm with the board that report content and frequency meet its oversight needs.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides content and recipients for each version

subtopics.isaca_rule: Same facts, different cuts: detail for those who act, the overall picture for those who oversee, and only what law and policy allow for outside parties. Versions differ in depth, never in substance.

exam_traps.trap: The board should receive the full detailed report for every engagement.
exam_traps.why: Communications should fit each recipient's needs. The board needs what it requires for oversight; detailed findings mainly serve the activity's management.

exam_traps.trap: A summary for senior management may soften a finding's rating.
exam_traps.why: Versions may differ in detail and format, but every version stays accurate and objective. A rating does not change by audience.

key_terms.definition: A person or group that is affected by, or cares about, what the organization does and how it turns out.
Any internal or external party that gives assurance, such as compliance, risk management or the external auditor.

subtopics.name: Already-Fixed Findings and Corrected Reports
subtopics.definition: Two special cases: a finding management fixed before the report was issued, and a significant error or omission found after issue.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Dropping a fixed finding hides what was wrong during the period reviewed. An uncorrected error leaves readers acting on wrong information.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 15.1): when management has started or completed action on a finding before issue, acknowledge that action in the final communication.
KaiSip's reading: the finding stays, because it records the condition found. Say whether internal auditors confirmed the fix or management reports it done.
Must (Standard 11.4 Errors and Omissions): the chief audit executive (CAE) promptly sends corrected information to every party that received the original.
Must: significance follows criteria agreed with the board.
Should: ask whether the error could have legal or regulatory effects, or change results or actions.
Should: the CAE and the board agree a protocol for corrections, and the CAE finds the error's cause and acts to prevent a repeat.

rows.label: Finding fixed before issue
cells: Report the finding and acknowledge the action taken
The usual recipients of the final communication

rows.label: Significant error found after issue
cells: Send corrected information promptly, then find and fix the cause
Everyone who received the original

subtopics.example: Two weeks after issuing a report on research grant spending at a university in Santiago, chief audit executive Ignacio learns that a finding named the wrong department as overspending. Under the criteria agreed with the audit committee this is significant, so Ignacio sends a correction to the dean, the rector and the committee, every original recipient, and reviews how the error slipped through.

review: Compare a corrected report's recipients with the original distribution
Inspect reports for findings fixed before issue but dropped
evidence: Significance criteria approved with the audit committee, with version dates
Original and corrected reports with their distribution records
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive agree a correction protocol and significance criteria with the board.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive judges significance against board-agreed criteria

subtopics.isaca_rule: A finding fixed before issue is reported with the fix acknowledged, not deleted. A significant error goes back out, promptly, to everyone who received the original, judged by board-agreed criteria; then the CAE fixes its cause.

exam_traps.trap: Management fixed the issue during fieldwork, so the finding can be removed from the report.
exam_traps.why: Must: actions taken before issue are acknowledged in the final communication (Standard 15.1). The fix is credited, not used to erase the condition the auditors found.

exam_traps.trap: A significant error is corrected by telling the board, since it oversees the function.
exam_traps.why: Must: the corrected information goes promptly to every recipient of the original (Standard 11.4), not only the board.

key_terms.definition: A mistake or gap in an issued report that meets the board-agreed criteria, such as one that changes results or has legal effect.
The method the chief audit executive agrees with the board for sending out corrected information.

subtopics.memory_aid: Fixed before issue: report it, credit the fix. Wrong after issue: correct it for everyone.

topics.overview: To say how serious findings are, internal auditors evaluate the controls in place, judge the residual risk, and rank findings with the chief audit executive's methodology. The overall result is often shown on a rating scale. This topic covers why the chief audit executive sets these methods: consistent results that the board can compare across engagements.
can_do: Recognize how existing controls are evaluated for design and effectiveness to reach residual risk
Describe why findings are aggregated and prioritized with one function-wide method
Describe what a rating scale for the overall assessment is for, and what it must not become

subtopics.name: From Controls to Residual Risk
subtopics.definition: Assessing residual risk means evaluating the controls in place for design and effectiveness, then judging how much risk remains despite them, to set a finding's significance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Significance rests on the risk the organization actually carries. Rating a finding on inherent risk, or on controls nobody tested, misstates how urgent the fix is.
how_it_works: Should (Standard 14.3): evaluate how well existing controls are designed and how well they work, then set the residual risk; judging significance from it is Part 2 (2B6.3).
Sound practice: judge design by walk-throughs and by matching each control to its risk; judge effectiveness by sampling, reperformance and observation (see 2A6.1 and 2A6.2).
Sound practice: count only controls that are adequately designed and shown to work; a failed or untested control reduces little.
Must (Standard 14.3): internal auditors prioritize findings with the chief audit executive's (CAE's) methodology.
KaiSip's reading: the CAE's part in residual risk is setting that method and approving the results; internal auditors do the evaluation.
subtopics.example: At a vaccine distributor in Hanoi, auditor Minh evaluates cold-storage controls. Tests show two of five freezer alarms were switched off. Minh counts only the working alarms and the tested backup generator, judges that the residual risk of spoiled stock still exceeds the company's tolerance, and rates the finding high on the function's scale.

review: Recalculate residual ratings counting only controls that passed testing
Sample findings for documented design and effectiveness evaluations
evidence: Control test results supporting each residual rating
Rating criteria set out in the function's methodology
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive tie residual risk rating criteria to the organization's risk tolerance.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides how to treat residual risk above tolerance

subtopics.isaca_rule: Residual risk comes after evaluating controls for design and effectiveness, counting only controls that work. Significance weighs likelihood and impact against tolerance, rated with the CAE's method so every engagement means the same thing.

exam_traps.trap: Rate the finding on the risk before controls, to be cautious.
exam_traps.why: That is inherent risk. Significance rests on residual risk, the risk left after evaluating the controls in place (Standard 14.3, considerations).

exam_traps.trap: A control described in the procedures manual reduces residual risk.
exam_traps.why: Only a control that is adequately designed and operating reduces risk. A documented control that is not performed leaves the risk in place.

key_terms.definition: The exposure still left once management's controls and other responses are in place.
The exposure an activity carries before counting anything management does about it.

subtopics.memory_aid: Test the controls, count only the working ones, then rate what is left.

subtopics.name: Aggregating and Prioritizing Findings
subtopics.definition: Aggregating means judging findings together for their combined weight; prioritizing means ranking each finding by significance so the most serious get attention first.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Readers and action owners have limited time. Ranking points them to what matters most, and looking across findings reveals weaknesses no single finding shows.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 14.3): prioritize each finding by significance using methodologies the chief audit executive (CAE) establishes, for consistency across engagements.
May: a rating or ranking can describe each finding's significance and help management order its action plans.
Must (Standard 14.5 Engagement Conclusions): the conclusion weighs the findings in aggregate; how auditors do that within one engagement is Part 2 (see 2B8.1).
Must (Standard 15.1): the assurance final communication shows each finding's significance and priority.
Must (Standard 11.3): across engagements, the CAE communicates themes, such as shared root causes, to the board and senior management in a timely way.
subtopics.example: At a logistics group in Johannesburg, chief audit executive Thandi notices that warehouse audits in three provinces each rated access-control findings as medium. Viewed together, they share one cause: a security contractor's weak onboarding of guards. Thandi reports the theme to the audit committee and senior management, and proposes an engagement on contractor management.

review: Compare ratings of similar findings across engagements for consistency
Inspect board reports for themes drawn from several engagements
evidence: Findings database with ratings and root causes
Methodology criteria for each priority level
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive run periodic calibration reviews of finding ratings across engagement teams.
audit_focus.decides: Management orders its action plans using the agreed priorities

subtopics.isaca_rule: Rank every finding by significance with the CAE's single method, then weigh them together for the conclusion. Across engagements, the CAE looks for themes and reports them to the board and senior management.

exam_traps.trap: The CAE should report a theme only once it has produced a high-rated finding.
exam_traps.why: Must: themes in governance, risk management and control go to the board and senior management in a timely way; a shared cause behind medium findings can be the point.

exam_traps.trap: A theme seen across units is reported only to the managers of those units.
exam_traps.why: Must: the CAE communicates themes, with insights, advice or conclusions, to the board and senior management (Standard 11.3).

key_terms.definition: Judging findings together, so their combined weight and any shared cause shape the overall conclusion.
A pattern, such as a shared root cause or a good practice, seen across several engagements.
How much a matter counts in its setting, weighing size as well as nature.

subtopics.name: Rating Scales for the Overall Assessment
subtopics.definition: A rating scale is a set of defined levels, such as satisfactory to unsatisfactory, that expresses the overall judgment on an activity's controls the same way in every engagement.
subtopics.why_it_matters: One word tells busy readers how serious the overall picture is, lets the board compare engagements, and shows trends over time.
how_it_works: May (Standard 14.5, considerations): the chief audit executive's (CAE's) methodology may provide a scale showing whether reasonable assurance exists that controls are effective.
May: example levels are satisfactory, partially satisfactory, needs improvement and unsatisfactory, each defined in the methodology.
Must (Standard 14.5): an assurance conclusion gives a judgment on the effectiveness of governance, risk management and control, acknowledging effective processes too.
May: add context on where impact falls; a finding can matter greatly to the activity yet little to the organization.
Must (Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior): never deliberately omit or minimize ratings; the considerations list doing so as discreditable conduct.
subtopics.example: At a hospital network in Toronto, chief audit executive Priya defines a four-level scale with criteria for each level. An audit of patient billing produces one high and two low findings that share a cause in the claims system. The engagement team rates billing controls 'needs improvement' and explains in the conclusion why the high finding drives the rating.

review: Reperform the overall rating for a sample of engagements
Trace rating changes between draft and final to a documented reason
evidence: Rating scale definitions in the methodology
Draft and final reports showing each rating's history
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive test rating consistency in internal quality assessments and refresh level descriptions.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive approves the rating in the final communication

subtopics.isaca_rule: A rating scale makes the overall judgment consistent and readable. It summarizes the auditors' evaluation, follows the CAE's defined criteria, and is never bargained with management or produced by counting findings.

exam_traps.trap: Management may ask for a better rating in exchange for faster action.
exam_traps.why: The rating reflects the auditors' evaluation against defined criteria. It is not traded for cooperation; a valid reason, such as new evidence, is needed to change it.

exam_traps.trap: Every engagement must use a four-level rating scale.
exam_traps.why: A rating scale is a may in the considerations, and the four levels are only an example. The must is a conclusion on effectiveness for assurance work.

key_terms.definition: A defined set of levels the function uses to express an overall assessment consistently.
Well-founded confidence, never certainty, that risk management and control give about meeting objectives.
The auditors' overall verdict on the engagement results, taken together.

subtopics.memory_aid: One scale, defined levels, the same meaning everywhere; never bargained.

topics.topic_name: When management accepts too much risk
topics.overview: Management may choose to live with a risk instead of acting on a finding; within the organization's limits that is its call. When the chief audit executive concludes that the accepted risk goes beyond the organization's risk appetite or risk tolerance, Standard 11.5 sets who must hear of it and in what order. This topic covers the test, the parties and the sequence.
can_do: Recognize the test for unacceptable risk: above the organization's risk appetite or risk tolerance
Recognize who takes part in communicating risk acceptance and what each party does
Put the steps for communicating risk acceptance in order, telling each must from each should

subtopics.name: The Test: Above Appetite or Tolerance
subtopics.definition: Unacceptable risk, under Standard 11.5, is a level of risk that management has accepted beyond the organization's risk appetite or risk tolerance, as the chief audit executive concludes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The yardstick is the organization's own limits, not the auditor's comfort; it keeps the chief audit executive from raising false alarms or staying silent.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 11.5 Communicating the Acceptance of Risks): the chief audit executive (CAE) communicates unacceptable levels of risk.
Must: the trigger is the CAE's conclusion, reached with professional judgment, that accepted risk goes beyond the organization's risk appetite or tolerance.
Should, where formal risk management exists: the CAE understands management's risk acceptance policies; the board, senior management and audit results show the limits.
May: the CAE spots acceptance in management's responses to findings and in slow progress on action plans (see 3D8).
May: impacts of risk beyond appetite include harm to reputation or people, major fines, misstatement, fraud or illegal acts, and blocked strategic objectives.
KaiSip's reading: the syllabus title speaks loosely of risk the organization cannot accept; apply Standard 11.5's test, appetite or tolerance.
subtopics.example: At an online lender in Jakarta, the board's appetite statement allows no lending to unverified borrowers. To speed approvals, the loans unit's management skips identity checks for small loans and accepts the fraud risk. Chief audit executive Dewi compares the decision with the appetite statement, concludes it goes beyond appetite, and starts the Standard 11.5 process.

review: Compare risk decisions in management responses with the appetite statement
Trace accepted risks above tolerance to a recorded escalation
evidence: Board-approved risk appetite and tolerance statements
Management responses declining recommended actions, with reasons
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management keep risk appetite and tolerance statements current and known to managers.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management may resolve it; if unresolved, the board decides how to address it

subtopics.isaca_rule: The yardstick is the organization's risk appetite or risk tolerance, never the auditor's comfort. Management may accept risk inside those limits; above them, the CAE must communicate it. Slow action can be acceptance too.

exam_traps.trap: The CAE should escalate any accepted risk the CAE personally finds too high.
exam_traps.why: The test is the organization's appetite or tolerance for risk. The CAE's judgment applies that yardstick; it does not replace it.

exam_traps.trap: Any risk management accepts is a problem internal audit must escalate.
exam_traps.why: Accepting risk within appetite and tolerance is a normal management decision. Only acceptance beyond those limits triggers Standard 11.5.

key_terms.definition: A knowing decision to bear a risk without further action.
How much risk, and which kinds, an organization is prepared to take for its strategy.
The band of results around an objective that the organization can live with.

subtopics.memory_aid: Their limits, not my comfort: appetite or tolerance.

subtopics.name: Who Takes Part
subtopics.definition: The parties to communicating risk acceptance are the chief audit executive, the management responsible for the risk, senior management and the board, each with a distinct role.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Raising the matter with the wrong party wastes time or bypasses people who could fix it. Knowing each role tells you who acts next and who never acts.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 11.5): the chief audit executive (CAE) concludes, communicates and escalates; internal auditors bring the facts.
Must: the CAE never resolves an accepted risk; senior management or, if unresolved, the board decides. This differs from helping settle a dispute over results (3D3.4).
Should: the management responsible for the risk hears the CAE's concerns first, explains its view and may agree an updated action plan.
Must: the CAE discusses the matter with senior management when accepted risk exceeds appetite or tolerance.
Must: the CAE escalates to the board if senior management has not resolved it. Per the considerations, the board decides how to address it with management.
May: the CAE seeks the board's agreement on how such risks are documented and communicated, possibly involving legal counsel or the head of compliance.

rows.label: Chief audit executive
cells: Concludes, communicates and escalates; never resolves the risk
Must

rows.label: Management responsible for the risk
cells: Hears concerns first, explains, may agree an updated plan
Should

rows.label: Senior management
cells: Discusses the matter with the CAE and may resolve it
Must

rows.label: Board
cells: Receives what stays unresolved and decides how to address it
Must escalate; the board's decision comes from the considerations

subtopics.example: At a chemicals firm in Rotterdam, plant management declines to fix an overdue safety-valve inspection, citing cost. Chief audit executive Sanne meets the plant director first, without agreement, then discusses it with the chief operating officer, who also declines. Judging the risk unresolved and above tolerance, Sanne takes it to the audit committee.

review: Trace escalated risks through each party's documented discussion
Compare escalation records with the board-agreed methodology
evidence: Dated meeting notes from each level the matter passed through
Board or committee minutes recording escalated risks
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive agree with the board a documented route for communicating accepted risks.
audit_focus.decides: The board chooses its response once the matter reaches it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Four parties, four roles: responsible management hears it first (should), senior management must discuss it, and the board hears what stays unresolved and decides. The CAE communicates and escalates; the CAE never resolves the risk.

exam_traps.trap: Once the board has the matter, the CAE should direct management's corrective action.
exam_traps.why: Must: resolving the risk is not the CAE's responsibility. The board decides how to address the concern with management.

exam_traps.trap: The internal auditor who found the risk should present it to senior management.
exam_traps.why: Communicating risk acceptance is the CAE's duty under Standard 11.5. The internal auditor brings the facts to the CAE.

key_terms.definition: The managers who own the risk in question and can act on it; the CAE should raise concerns with them first.
The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board.

subtopics.name: The Order of the Steps
subtopics.definition: The risk acceptance sequence is the order the chief audit executive follows: conclude, raise with responsible management, discuss with senior management, then escalate to the board if still unresolved.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Skipping a step bypasses people who could resolve the matter. Stopping too early leaves the board unaware of a risk beyond its limits.
how_it_works: Must, step 1 (Standard 11.5): the chief audit executive (CAE) concludes that management has accepted risk beyond appetite or tolerance.
Should, step 2: the CAE takes it up directly with the responsible management, to share concerns, understand their view and agree an updated action plan.
Must, step 3: if no agreement is reached, the CAE discusses the matter with senior management.
Must, step 4: if the CAE determines senior management has not resolved it, the CAE escalates it to the board; per the considerations, the board decides how to respond.
Should: document the risk, the concern, management's reason for not acting, who accepted the risk, and the date of each discussion.
subtopics.example: Chief audit executive Kofi at a mobile-money firm in Accra learns that the compliance unit has stopped screening transfers below a threshold, beyond the board's tolerance. Kofi meets the compliance head, who refuses to restart. Kofi then raises it with the chief executive, who backs the compliance head. Kofi records each discussion and takes the matter to the board's risk committee.

review: Trace each escalated matter through the steps in order
Inspect escalation records for the name of whoever accepted the risk
evidence: Dated records of each discussion and its outcome
Board-agreed methodology for communicating accepted risks
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive record each step, the person accepting the risk and the dates.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides how the unresolved risk is addressed

subtopics.isaca_rule: Order matters: responsible management first (should), senior management next (must), then the board if the CAE judges it unresolved (must). Senior management's own acceptance does not end it while the CAE judges the risk unresolved.

exam_traps.trap: Go straight to the board, since the board set the risk appetite.
exam_traps.why: Standard 11.5 requires discussion with senior management first, and the considerations say to raise it with the responsible management before that. The board hears what stays unresolved.

exam_traps.trap: Senior management formally accepted the risk, so the matter is closed.
exam_traps.why: If the CAE determines senior management has not resolved a risk beyond appetite or tolerance, it must go to the board.

key_terms.definition: A revised plan, with new steps or dates, agreed when the original plan has stalled or fallen short.
The documented risk, concern, reasons, the name of whoever accepted it, and the dates of each discussion.

subtopics.memory_aid: Conclude, responsible manager, senior management, board. The board decides; the CAE never resolves.

topics.overview: An engagement is not finished when the report goes out. Internal auditors must confirm that management has carried out its actions, using a methodology the chief audit executive sets: ask about progress, assess on a risk basis, and keep a tracking system current. The results feed reports to the board and senior management.
can_do: Recognize internal audit's duty to follow up and track management's actions, and where that duty stops
Distinguish inquiry, follow-up assessment and tracking, scaling each to the finding's significance
Describe how past-due items, alternative plans and closures are handled in the tracking system

subtopics.name: Internal Audit's Duty to Follow Up
subtopics.definition: Follow-up is internal audit's duty to confirm, by an established method, that management has carried out the recommendations or action plans agreed after an engagement.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An action that is never carried out leaves the risk in place. Follow-up tells the board and senior management whether issues actually get fixed.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 15.2 Confirming the Implementation of Recommendations or Action Plans): internal auditors confirm that management has implemented actions, following an established methodology.
Must (Standard 9.3 Methodologies): the chief audit executive (CAE) establishes the function's methodologies; the considerations list monitoring and confirming action plans among them.
Should (Standard 14.4): internal auditors work with management on actions but never own them; management implements and auditors confirm.
Must (Standard 8.1): the CAE reports monitoring results to the board and senior management.
May: a tracking system supports those reports.
May (Standard 15.2, considerations): in some circumstances regulators require reporting on management's action plans.
subtopics.example: Six months after an audit of tenant deposits at a housing association in Glasgow, auditor Fiona asks each action owner for an update, tests the two high-priority actions and updates the tracking system. One owner asks Fiona to write the new deposit procedure. Fiona declines, explains that the procedure is management's to write, and offers examples of good practice instead.

review: Trace actions in issued reports to entries in the tracking system
Compare closed items with the confirmation evidence held
evidence: Tracking system extract with status and confirmation dates
Action status reports presented to the board
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive report open and overdue actions to the board and senior management on a set schedule.
audit_focus.decides: Management carries the work through and answers for delays
