subtopics.isaca_rule: Confirming implementation is internal audit's must; implementing is management's. The CAE's methodology sets how, and the monitoring results go to the board and senior management.

exam_traps.trap: Once the report is issued, follow-up is management's job alone.
exam_traps.why: Management implements, but internal auditors must confirm implementation following an established methodology (Standard 15.2).

exam_traps.trap: To speed things up, the auditor should carry out an overdue action.
exam_traps.why: Implementing would take on management's responsibility and impair objectivity when the area is next assessed. Auditors confirm; management acts.

key_terms.definition: Internal audit's work after an engagement to confirm that agreed actions were carried out.
What follow-up shows about the status of management's actions, reported to the board and senior management.

subtopics.name: Inquire, Assess, Track
subtopics.definition: The three follow-up steps are asking management about progress, performing risk-based follow-up assessments, and keeping each action's status current in a tracking system.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Each step gives different comfort. Inquiry is quick but rests on management's word, assessment gives evidence, and tracking keeps the whole picture visible.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 15.2): the methodology includes inquiring about progress, performing follow-up assessments on a risk basis, and updating status in a tracking system.
Must: the extent of these procedures considers the significance of the finding.
Should: the methodology sets criteria for when to perform follow-up assessments that confirm actions have effectively addressed findings.
May: assess completed actions selectively, by significance.
KaiSip's reading: test high-priority actions; for minor ones, inquiry backed by evidence may be enough.
Sound practice: an assessment checks that the action works, not only that it exists, for example by sampling transactions since it began.

rows.label: Inquiry
cells: Management's account of status and any delay
Open actions, scaled to significance

rows.label: Assessment
cells: Evidence the action was implemented and addresses the finding
Chosen by risk; most for significant findings

rows.label: Tracking
cells: A current record of open, past-due and closed actions
Every action, kept current

subtopics.example: At a seaport in Valparaiso, auditor Camila follows up eight actions from a cargo-security audit. Camila asks every owner for status, then tests the two high-priority actions by sampling gate logs since the new badge checks began. The six minor actions are closed on the owners' evidence, as the methodology allows, and Camila updates all eight in the tracking system.

review: Sample closed high-priority actions for a follow-up assessment
Reconcile closed statuses with supporting files for a sample of items
evidence: Retest results for sampled high-priority actions
Change log showing who altered each item's status and when
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set criteria for which completed actions need a follow-up assessment.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive sets follow-up criteria in the methodology

subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask, assess, track, scaled to significance (must). Follow-up assessments may be selective by risk; KaiSip's reading: test significant findings' actions, and inquiry backed by evidence may do for minor ones. The tracking system holds every action's status.

exam_traps.trap: Every completed action should be fully retested before it is closed.
exam_traps.why: Must: the extent of follow-up considers significance, and assessments may be selective by risk. Fully retesting minor actions wastes effort.

exam_traps.trap: A significant finding can be closed when management emails that it is done.
exam_traps.why: Inquiry rests on management's word, and the extent of follow-up must consider significance (Standard 15.2). KaiSip's reading: a significant finding gets a follow-up assessment before it closes.

key_terms.definition: Testing done after management reports an action complete, to confirm it was implemented and addresses the finding.
A tool, such as a database or spreadsheet, that records each action's owner, due date and status.

subtopics.memory_aid: Ask about all, test by risk, track everything.

subtopics.name: Past-Due Items, Alternative Plans and Closure
subtopics.definition: Managing the tracking record means flagging past-due actions, tracking any alternative plan internal auditors accept, and closing items only once implementation is confirmed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An item closed because its date passed, or a better alternative rejected because it differs from the original, gives the board a false picture of risk.
how_it_works: May (Standard 15.2): use software, a spreadsheet or a system that shows open and past-due actions, with automatic reminders as due dates approach.
Should: if management chooses an alternative plan that internal auditors agree is as good or better, track the alternative to completion.
Must: for actions not progressing by their dates, internal auditors obtain and document management's explanation and discuss it with the chief audit executive (see 3D8).
KaiSip's reading: close an item when the methodology's confirmation is done, never because its due date passed or a new date was set.
Sound practice: record the reason for any change of date or plan, and which manager approved it.
subtopics.example: At a wind-farm operator in Aarhus, management drops a planned manual check of turbine maintenance logs and instead installs software that flags missed services automatically. Auditor Mads reviews the software's reports, agrees the new approach addresses the finding better, and updates the tracking system to follow the new plan to completion.

review: Sample past-due items for a documented management explanation
Inspect closures for confirmation evidence rather than elapsed dates
evidence: Tracking system aging report of past-due actions
Records of alternative plans accepted, with reasons
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive require a documented basis for every closure and every date change.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses its plan and owns any change of date

subtopics.isaca_rule: The tracking system must tell the truth: past-due shows as past-due, a sound alternative plan is tracked in place of the original, and nothing closes until confirmed. A passing date is not completion.

exam_traps.trap: Management's alternative plan differs from the agreed one, so the action is recorded as not implemented.
exam_traps.why: Should: if internal auditors agree the alternative is satisfactory or better, its progress is tracked until completion (Standard 15.2).

exam_traps.trap: The due date has passed and management says it is nearly done, so mark it closed.
exam_traps.why: Closing needs confirmation under the methodology. A late action gets management's documented explanation and is discussed with the chief audit executive.

key_terms.definition: An action not completed by its agreed date, flagged in the tracking system.
A different plan management chooses instead of the original, tracked if auditors agree it is as good or better.

subtopics.memory_aid: A passed date is not a done action.

topics.topic_name: Escalating actions that were not completed
topics.overview: When management misses its dates or does too little, the matter moves up a set route. Internal auditors obtain and document management's explanation and take it to the chief audit executive, who decides whether the delay amounts to accepting risk beyond tolerance. If it does, the Standard 11.5 route applies, up to the board.
can_do: Recognize who takes part when an action plan is late or inadequate, and what each party does
Put the escalation steps in order, from the missed date to the board
Recognize when delay or inaction amounts to accepting risk beyond tolerance

subtopics.name: Who Takes Part When Actions Slip
subtopics.definition: The parties to escalation are the internal auditors following up, the management that owns the action, the chief audit executive, senior management and the board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Each party has one job in the chain. Mixing them up leads to auditors bypassing the chief audit executive, or the chief audit executive doing management's work.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 15.2): internal auditors obtain and document management's explanation for the delay, then discuss the issue with the chief audit executive (CAE).
Should (Standard 14.4): the management that owns the action explains the delay, may commit to an updated plan, and stays responsible for implementing.
Must (Standard 15.2): the CAE judges whether, through the delay or inaction, senior management has accepted a risk above the risk tolerance.
KaiSip's reading: the late action is the owning manager's; Standard 15.2 asks whether senior management, by letting the delay stand, has accepted the risk.
Must (Standard 8.1): the board and senior management receive monitoring results, overdue actions included, in the CAE's regular reports; escalation steps are in 3D8.2.

rows.label: Internal auditors
cells: Document the explanation; take it to the CAE
Go to the board or do the action

rows.label: Management that owns the action
cells: Explains the delay and implements
Hand the action to internal audit

rows.label: Chief audit executive
cells: Judges whether delay means accepted risk; escalates
Set dates or resolve the risk

rows.label: Senior management
cells: Discusses it with the CAE; may resolve it
Close it while the CAE judges it unresolved

rows.label: Board
cells: Decides how to address an unresolved matter with management
Get the escalation before senior management has discussed it (routine overdue reports still reach it)

subtopics.example: At a regional bank in Porto Alegre, an action to remove dormant system accounts is four months late. Auditor Bruno asks the IT manager why, records that the team was moved to a merger project, and takes the explanation to chief audit executive Helena, who now has to judge whether the delay means excess risk has been accepted.

review: Sample overdue actions for a documented explanation from management
Trace overdue significant actions to the chief audit executive's recorded judgment
evidence: Tracking system aging report with explanations attached
Committee papers listing late actions and their age
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set in the methodology when overdue actions are referred and reported.
audit_focus.decides: The owning manager still delivers the fix, however late

subtopics.isaca_rule: Auditors document the reason and take it to the CAE; the CAE judges whether delay means accepted excess risk; if so, senior management and then the board hear it. Management owns the action throughout.

exam_traps.trap: An auditor whose follow-up requests are ignored should write directly to the audit committee.
exam_traps.why: Must: the auditor obtains and documents management's explanation and discusses it with the CAE, who judges the matter and escalates it if needed.

exam_traps.trap: Every missed due date means management has accepted the risk.
exam_traps.why: The CAE determines whether delay or inaction amounts to acceptance of risk beyond tolerance; a short slip with a credible new plan may not.

key_terms.definition: Management not taking the agreed steps at all, as distinct from taking them late.
Passing a matter to a higher authority because the current level cannot, or should not, settle it.

subtopics.name: The Escalation Sequence
subtopics.definition: The escalation sequence is the ordered route a late or inadequate action takes: from the missed date, through the chief audit executive's judgment, to senior management and the board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam questions test the next step. Each step gives the people closest to the problem a chance to fix it before it goes higher.
how_it_works: Must, step 1 (Standard 15.2): keep the tracking system current, so past-due actions show.
Must, step 2: internal auditors obtain and document management's explanation and discuss it with the chief audit executive (CAE).
Must, step 3 (Standard 15.2): the CAE judges whether the delay or inaction amounts to accepting risk beyond the risk tolerance.
Should, step 4 (Standard 11.5): if so, the CAE first raises it with the responsible management, seeking an updated plan.
Must, step 5: if no agreement is reached, the CAE discusses the matter with senior management.
Must, step 6: if the CAE determines senior management has not resolved it, the CAE escalates to the board; per the considerations, the board decides how to respond.
subtopics.example: At a Hyderabad drug maker, a batch-record fix is six months late. Auditor Kavya documents the plant head's explanation and briefs chief audit executive Arjun, who judges it accepted risk beyond tolerance. Arjun meets the plant head (no new date), then the chief operating officer (deferred again), and escalates to the audit committee.

review: Trace a sample of escalated actions through each step and date
Compare time spent at each step with the methodology's limits
evidence: Dated records of explanations, discussions and escalations
Board minutes recording escalated overdue actions
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive agree escalation timing for overdue significant actions with the board.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides how to address an unresolved risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Climb in order: explanation documented and taken to the CAE; the CAE's judgment on accepted risk beyond tolerance; then responsible management (should), senior management (must) and the board if unresolved (must).

exam_traps.trap: Wait for the next scheduled engagement in the area to look at the late action.
exam_traps.why: Must: a late action is followed up now. The explanation is documented and discussed with the CAE, who decides whether escalation is needed.

exam_traps.trap: The CAE should set a firm new deadline and order management to meet it.
exam_traps.why: Management owns the plan and its dates. The CAE may agree an updated plan with management, and escalates if risk beyond tolerance has been accepted.

key_terms.definition: The rules the board sets with the chief audit executive for which issues reach the board, such as significant risks above its tolerance.
The agreed order of parties a matter passes through, set in the methodology and agreed with the board.

subtopics.memory_aid: Late, explain, CAE, owner again, senior management, board. Auditors document; the CAE escalates; the board decides.

subtopics.name: Delay or Accepted Risk: Reading the Signs
subtopics.definition: Judging delay means the chief audit executive deciding whether a late or weak action is a manageable slip or a sign that management has accepted risk beyond tolerance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Treating every slip as risk acceptance floods the board. Treating none as acceptance lets serious risks sit for years.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 15.2): the chief audit executive (CAE) determines whether delay or inaction means senior management has accepted risk beyond the risk tolerance.
May (Standard 11.5, considerations): insufficient progress on action plans can lead the CAE to conclude that risk beyond appetite or tolerance has been accepted.
KaiSip's reading: weigh the finding's significance, how long and how often dates slipped, whether interim measures hold the risk, and whether a credible new plan exists.
KaiSip's reading: Standard 15.2 says risk tolerance and Standard 11.5 says appetite or tolerance; each is kept as written, and they describe one test.
Sound practice: document the judgment and its basis. If acceptance is concluded, follow the Standard 11.5 route (see 3D6.3).

rows.label: Progress
cells: Work started, short delay, clear reason
Little or no work, repeated delays

rows.label: Plan
cells: A credible updated plan with owner, date and funding
No new plan, or one that keeps moving

rows.label: Interim position
cells: Temporary measures hold the risk within tolerance
Exposure stays beyond tolerance meanwhile

subtopics.example: Two actions are late at a frozen-food exporter in Bangkok. A new stock-count procedure slipped a month because scanners arrived late, and a funded new date is set. Fixing a cold-room alarm has slipped three times with no plan, while spoilage risk stays beyond tolerance. Chief audit executive Somchai keeps tracking the first and starts the Standard 11.5 route for the second.

review: Compare repeatedly extended due dates with escalation records
Inspect the documented basis for each delay judgment
evidence: Tracking history showing every due date change
Recorded judgments on overdue significant actions
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set criteria for when repeated slippage triggers a risk acceptance review.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management, then the board, respond if acceptance is concluded

subtopics.isaca_rule: Delay can be a decision. The CAE judges it by the finding's significance, the pattern of slippage, interim protection and the credibility of any new plan, and documents the judgment; acceptance beyond tolerance then follows Standard 11.5.

exam_traps.trap: As long as management keeps setting new dates, the action is in progress and needs no escalation.
exam_traps.why: Repeated delay or inaction can amount to accepting risk beyond tolerance. The CAE must judge it (Standard 15.2), not track new dates forever.

exam_traps.trap: Any delay on a high-priority action goes straight to the board.
exam_traps.why: Not as an escalation. The CAE first judges whether the delay means risk acceptance, and senior management is engaged before the board (Standard 11.5); routine status reports are separate.

key_terms.definition: A temporary step that limits a risk while the permanent action is completed.
Repeated movement of an action's due date without the work being done.

subtopics.memory_aid: Short slip with a plan: track it. Repeated slip, no plan: possible risk acceptance.

key_terminologies.Final communication: The communication issued at the end of an engagement with its results, often a written report.
key_terminologies.Closing communication: A discussion before the final communication, also called an exit conference, where auditors and management finalize the results.
key_terminologies.Scope limitation: A condition in an assurance engagement, such as restricted access, that prevents the planned work.
key_terminologies.Conformance: Meeting the requirements of the Global Internal Audit Standards.
key_terminologies.Nonconformance: A requirement of the Standards that was not met; it is documented and disclosed as the Standards direct.
key_terminologies.Recommendation: An action internal auditors propose to close a gap, reduce a risk or improve the activity under review.
key_terminologies.Action plan: Management's stated steps to deal with a finding, with a named owner and a target date.
key_terminologies.Root cause: The deeper reason a gap exists, as opposed to its visible symptom.
key_terminologies.Mutual understanding: Both sides see the facts and their meaning the same way, even if they differ on what to do.
key_terminologies.Valid reason: A sound basis for changing results, such as new evidence or a factual error, as opposed to pressure or preference.
key_terminologies.Dissemination: Sending a final communication to its chosen recipients, in the form the chief audit executive decides.
key_terminologies.Significant error or omission: A mistake or gap in an issued report that meets the board-agreed criteria, such as one that changes results or has legal effect.
key_terminologies.Residual risk: The exposure still left once management's controls and other responses are in place.
key_terminologies.Inherent risk: The exposure an activity carries before counting anything management does about it.
key_terminologies.Aggregation: Judging findings together, so their combined weight and any shared cause shape the overall conclusion.
key_terminologies.Theme: A pattern, such as a shared root cause or a good practice, seen across several engagements.
key_terminologies.Rating scale: A defined set of levels the function uses to express an overall assessment consistently.
key_terminologies.Engagement conclusion: The auditors' overall verdict on the engagement results, taken together.
key_terminologies.Risk acceptance: A knowing decision to bear a risk without further action.
key_terminologies.Risk appetite: How much risk, and which kinds, an organization is prepared to take for its strategy.
key_terminologies.Risk tolerance: The band of results around an objective that the organization can live with.
key_terminologies.Responsible management: The managers who own the risk in question and can act on it; the CAE should raise concerns with them first.
key_terminologies.Follow-up: Internal audit's work after an engagement to confirm that agreed actions were carried out.
key_terminologies.Follow-up assessment: Testing done after management reports an action complete, to confirm it was implemented and addresses the finding.
key_terminologies.Tracking system: A tool, such as a database or spreadsheet, that records each action's owner, due date and status.
key_terminologies.Alternative action plan: A different plan management chooses instead of the original, tracked if auditors agree it is as good or better.
key_terminologies.Escalation: Passing a matter to a higher authority because the current level cannot, or should not, settle it.
key_terminologies.Interim measure: A temporary step that limits a risk while the permanent action is completed.
